  b.billable_fe_o11y_sessions,
  b.billable_fe_o11y_sessions_delta,
  b.billable_sm_checks,

  b.hg_datasource_cnts,
  b.integrations,
  b.arr_sparkline_values,
  b.hm_sparkline_values,

options.content:
A hybrid panel: Semantic Layer + SQL

New tables tend to land in the warehouse faster than the semantic layer can model them. When that happens, dashboard authors need an escape hatch — a way to query those raw tables directly without blocking on the semantic layer catching up.

But they also want everything that can come from the semantic layer to come from the semantic layer, because that is the single source of truth, and it is what powers cross-panel filtering, governed measures, and value consistency with the rest of the dashboard.

How this panel is wired

  • semantic_layer_data (hidden) — the governed account universe (account_id, account_name) pulled through the territory_navigator view. AdHoc filters on the datasource are automatically injected, so this panel cross-filters with every other semantic-layer panel on the dashboard.
  • sql_data (hidden) — the org-level facts (org_slug, arr, billable_users, sparklines, and so on) pulled straight from rpt_self_serve_territory_navigator_orgs.
  • joined — a server-side Grafana SQL Expression that INNER JOINs the two on account_id, so Cube decides which accounts to show and PostgreSQL supplies every fact for each of their orgs. Grafana SQL Expressions let any two data source queries be blended this way, with the combined schema defined at query time.

Why this pattern is valuable

A semantic layer is the right place for trusted, governed metrics — consistent definitions, centralized access control, cross-panel filtering that just works. But a semantic layer that forces you to wait for a model update every time a new warehouse table appears becomes a bottleneck.

Grafana gives you both halves in the same dashboard: any semantic layer datasource for the governed half, any of the many SQL datasources — Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Athena, Redshift, and more — for the raw half, and SQL Expressions to blend them server-side.

When a column proves useful enough to deserve governance, promote it into the semantic layer and trim the SQL Expression. The blend shrinks toward pure semantic-layer queries over time — but the escape hatch stays available for whatever ships next.
